subtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN U.S. ARMED FORCES PROCUREMENT REGULATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN U.S. ARMED FORCES PROCUREMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to
make a statement on "buy American" regulations. As a result of our discussions with United States authorities regarding production sharing, the United States government has now made important changes in its armed services procurement regulations. These changes relate to the application of the buy American act to United States defence purchases in Canada. Their effect will be to give Canadian defence industry a much greater opportunity to share in the production of military equipment for the United States armed forces.
Under the new regulations the three United States services have adopted a common approach, and Canadian businessmen will no longer need to keep themselves informed on three different interpretations of the buy American act.
The key provision of this new approach is that Canadian supplies which relate to specific programs of mutual interest to the two governments will be exempt from all the limitations which are normally imposed under the buy American act. Canadian proposals to supply these goods to the United States services will be accepted on the same basis as American bids, giving Canadian sources an equal opportunity with American sources to compete for these orders.
The programs and equipment to which this total exemption will apply are being identified by the United States services in close consultation with my own officials. They will be designated in lists which will be issued by each of the services individually. It is our expectation that these lists will encompass such a wide range of items that Canadian defence industry will find ample scope to participate. These lists will be kept open, and it is the intention that they should be modified from time to time on the basis of continuing consultation.
Canadian manufacturers who are interested in supplying products which are not on the exempt lists will also find their opportunities improved under the new regulations. Canadian tenders or proposals to supply such goods have usually, in the past, been subject to the addition of several percentage differentials in the comparison of bids. Henceforth only the United States tariff will be added to a Canadian bid where non-exempt items are involved.
A third feature of the new regulations is that the total exemption from the buy American restrictions Will also apply to any component parts of the equipment included in

Defence Production
the exempt lists. This means that Canadian manufactures of such components, including a large number of our smaller industries, may find opportunities for taking part in these programs regardless of whether the prime contracts are awarded to Canadian or American firms. Canadian manufacturers of components may in fact find opportunities for sales to United States contractors even outside the range of exempt equipment. Under the regulations any United States defence contractor supplying non-exempt goods may buy up to 50 per cent of the material content of those goods from Canada and still enjoy the status of a domestic source.
I regard these new regulations as further evidence of the growing co-operation between Canada and the United States in defence production sharing, and welcome the promise they give of a greater share for Canadian defence industry in programs designed for our common defence.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN U.S. ARMED FORCES PROCUREMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure members of the house will have listened with great interest to the statement made by the minister, and will hope that the changes which have been made in the regulations will work out in practice so that Canadian industry will be able to share in the production of military equipment for the United States armed forces, as I understand from the minister is intended. Perhaps this statement may serve to remove some of the anxiety created by certain statements from Washington by members of the administration there, that this sharing was to take place only in respect of the production of military equipment for use by United States armed forces in Canada.
Perhaps I might also add, Mr. Speaker, that this change underlines the desirability of following up these matters in Washington through appropriate agencies of the Canadian government there. The minister will no doubt recall that in former years there was a special office for the purpose attached to the Canadian embassy, I think, in Washington, and this change underlines the importance of facilities of that kind in Washington which can be of great assistance to Canadian industry.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN U.S. ARMED FORCES PROCUREMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any move that will bring about an increased proportion of defence production orders for Canadian firms is, of course, welcome. The value of the changes that have been made will be known only in the course of time. Whether or not Canadian firms, being much smaller than United States firms, will in fact be able to compete on an equal basis is something that we shall have to determine in the light of events in the future. We

would prefer some general arrangement whereby Canadian industries would be assured a proportionate share of production orders, and we hope that the relaxation of these restrictions will lead to that end.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR USE OF DORMITORIES BY INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the relevant section of the Penitentiary Act that the bill seeks to amend is subsection 4 of section 66, which says that every inmate "shall, except in case of sickness, be kept in a cell by himself at night." There is no provision in the act to vary this arrangement, but for quite a number of years now the arrangement has been varied and dormitories have been in use in our penitentiaries. The amendment merely seeks to give the minister and the commissioner of penitentiaries statutory authority to do what they have been doing for the past number of years.

10. Agricultural Stabilization Act administration, $103,710.

Vote No. 10 is for the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I have had produced for me some statistics as to the quantity of agricultural products being held by the

board under this act. I am wondering if the minister could produce for the committee the quantities of various products that are presently being held by the board. There are some very substantial quantities, representing some $70 million or thereabouts as at the end of December. I wonder if the minister has some up to date figures, and whether he could tell the committee just what position the board is taking so far as the disposal of these various products is concerned.

The latest figures I have in my folder are those I had for the information of the committee some three weeks ago. This particular return was dated April 6, and as of that time the amounts of commodities held by the board were as follows: butter, 50,400,000 pounds; dry skim milk, 64,010,000; eggs, in shell, 154,000 cases; B.C. tomatoes, 86,000 cases; raspberries, B.C., frozen, 2,900,000 pounds; raspberries, B.C., in SOo, 291,000 pounds; hogs, pork cuts, 48,100,000 pounds.

There seems to have been a huge increase in the quantity of shell eggs on hand as compared with December 31. The record I have for December 31, 1958, shows the board held 3,108 cases of shell eggs at that date. The minister now says the quantity has risen to 154,000 cases. I wonder if he could give us the quantity of shell eggs held by the board a year ago? In other words, could he give us some idea whether or not this is an abnormal quantity which is being held at this time?
The quantity of pork products on hand on December 31, 1958, was 8,405,251 pounds. If I understand the minister correctly the quantity on hand today is in excess of 48 million pounds, an increase of six times in a period of a very few months. I wonder if the minister would care to comment on the reason for this tremendous accumulation of pork products, and say whether this is the reason the government is changing its buying supports. Does the government feel that the board has now on hand an unumanageable quantitiy of pork products; can he explain whether this quantity of 48 million pounds may be increased in the near future, and can he also tell the committee what method the government intends to adopt in order to dispose of it?

As far as eggs are concerned, we have just in the last month or a little longer come into the heavy production season. This is the period of the year during which we are taking the surplus oil the market and when we are required to buy eggs. During the fall and winter months production is, of course, down, and we are not required to buy, in normal circumstances 66968-9-205
Supply-Agriculture
at least. As far as a comparison with last year is concerned, egg production has increased quite materially. We have not the figures showing by what percentage production has increased this year over last year, but it is up by a considerable amount. Thus we have been buying more eggs this year than we were buying last year.
As far as pork cuts are concerned, the hon. member is aware, of course, that during recent months we have had the heaviest run of hogs on the Canadian market that we have ever had in peacetime, almost as high as we had during the war, in 1944, when the raising of hogs was being encouraged by every means possible in order to produce food for Britain and help the war effort. The result of this extremely heavy run of hogs has been a great deal more pork coming on the market than the market could absorb, and thus we have been obliged during recent weeks to buy heavily in order to maintain the support price of $25 a hundred. The run will now, of course, begin to slow down, and during July and August we should be able to dispose of some of the pork we now hold.

I wonder if the minister could comment on the quantity of eggs which the board now holds and say whether it poses great difficulties for the board. The floor prices on eggs, in my opinion are very low, particularly when the producer is a long distance from the central markets, and when farmers are unable to take their eggs directly to a candling station the prices paid to producers are very low. As a consumer, during the session in Ottawa I find that grade A large are usually between 55 cents and 60 cents a dozen. However, the farmers in my constituency are selling fresh ungraded eggs at between 18 cents and 20 cents a dozen. There certainly seems to be something wrong with our whole pricing and transportation policy when the producers in one area are getting only 18 cents a dozen and the consumers in another are paying three times that sum.
I hope that at the very least the government will maintain the floor price on eggs. We are seeing a very substantial erosion of the floor prices under this act as is clear from recent announcements. The trend now seems to be toward lower support prices, and I should appreciate any assurance the minister can give me that the surplus of eggs on hand is not unmanageable and that at least for the next 12 months, or for a given period, the present floor price will be the minimum.

As the hon. member is well aware, I am not in a position to give any assurance of the kind he has just mentioned. When the support price on eggs is decided it will be announced in the house, and that

Supply-Agriculture
will be in a week or so. As I say, I am not in a position to announce it now. I may say that the advisory committee to the stabilization board met yesterday and is meeting again today, and eggs happen to be one of the things they are considering and with regard to which we will be getting their advice. That will be today, I imagine.
The price for the coming year will be announced in the house some time next week, I expect, or at least in the week following.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member for Assiniboia made a statement which I think can only mislead the poultry industry. I am not saying he intended to do that, but that could be the only possible result. I am referring to his statement that there must be something wrong with the system when producers are getting 18 cents a dozen and consumers are paying 50 cents a dozen.
The main thing to remember is that these are not the same eggs, not the same graded eggs. The producer in Saskatchewan is getting 30 cents a dozen for his grade A large eggs, and we are buying those eggs in Montreal and Toronto, packed in wooden cases and so forth at 44 cents a dozen, with appropriate differentials on account of freight to other points. In any event, the producer of these large eggs is getting 30 cents a dozen, and these eggs are selling, as the hon. member mentioned with regard to his experience in Ottawa, at prices from 50 cents to 55 cents a dozen.
Those are grade A large eggs. The eggs which are sold in Saskatchewan at 18 cents a dozen are ungraded, as the hon. member said, and in a very large number of cases they contain a considerable proportion of grade B eggs, cracked eggs and so on I might add that for grade B eggs there is, in effect, no real market in Canada; the producers have to take more or less what anybody will give them. Bakers buy them for use in bakery products, but there is really no market which will give any return for them.
In Saskatchewan, unfortunately, the proportion of eggs which meet grade A standards is very small in comparison with other provinces. I do not have the exact figures here but I know, speaking from memory, that in the eastern provinces grade A eggs constitute 90 per cent and upwards of the total production whereas in Saskatchewan they run at 50 per cent and in some cases at only 25 per cent. Therefore the people who deliver eggs of poor quality really have no right to complain when they do not receive grade A large prices, because they are producing a different grade of egg altogether.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could say what regulations are in effect to assure the producer that he is being

paid a price based on an accurate grade. I have seen in the newspapers instances where people in western Canada have purchased eggs out of the packing company warehouse, and for example cases of grade A eggs have been resold to the very same company and the majority of eggs have been graded as B, C or rots.
I have often said this and I repeat it now; that no matter what criticism one makes from time to time of our method of handling grain there is at least a good grading system and the producer has some protection. What protection is there for the egg producer when he ships a case of eggs? Where is the assurance that he is not being deprived of a price for his eggs based on the minister's floor price because his eggs have been undergraded? Is there any policing arrangement? Are there inspectors to make certain not just that the board buys eggs of the proper grade but that the producer is given an accurate grade and is paid whatever price there may be, low as it is?

Mr. Chairman, we have inspectors who inspect regularly all of the egg grading stations in Canada. Very seldom do they find that eggs are being improperly graded. Of course there are bound to be some cases where eggs have been improperly graded just as there are cases where people complain that their wheat has been improperly graded, and so on. The number of cases that our inspectors find in which eggs are being improperly graded is very small.
We have had complaints along the line the hon. member mentioned. I have had several people write and tell me that this is what happened. However, I have yet to receive what you might call conclusive proof adduced in connection with this matter though, as I said, there is no question but that mistakes are bound to be made sometimes. At a particular egg grading station eggs might be consistently undergraded for a time, but our inspectors inspect regularly and find very few cases of this type.
Mr. Chairman, when an egg buying firm undergrades eggs, does it break any Canadian law? Could the minister reply to my question?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
What law?

The provincial grading
legislation and our federal Agricultural Products Standards Act.
Has there ever been a prosecution under the federal standards act for the improper grading of eggs and, if so, when?
I am informed that action would be taken under the provincial statute.

There is the trouble, you see. The taxpayers of this country put up the money to keep a floor price under eggs and this government is doing what the former government did in this field and about which the Conservative members criticized them most strongly namely providing a floor price to the packers rather than to the producers of eggs. Under the policy of this government the packing companies in some instances, I would suggest on the face of the minister's statement, are undergrading eggs. These companies are underwritten by the taxpayers, and the producer has no recourse under any federal statute. He cannot claim against the packer who is beating and gypping him as far as egg grades are concerned.
That is a serious accusation.

That is not a serious accusation but a statement of fact. I have had many businessmen in our communities bring to me local receipts which showed that a very insignificant percentage of eggs are being graded A, a ridiculously low percentage. While there may be producers of eggs who are not as careful as they should be and who do not produce anywhere near the 90 per cent of grade A eggs which the minister says are produced in the province of Ontario, nevertheless I do not believe that when a local dealer is handling hundreds upon hundreds of cases of eggs there could possibly be an almost absence of grade A eggs. As the minister has stated, there is no recourse under the law by which the producer can make a claim for proper egg grading and proper prices.
I brought to the minister's attention on a previous occasion the alleged combine by the western egg producers' association. I was pleased that steps were taken at least with respect to grade A extra large eggs to provide that the packers should pay on any eggs that are graded A extra large the support price that was intended. I hope the minister, instead of taking offence at what I have been saying, will look into the question and see whether or not penalties could be provided under the stabilization act or some other legislation that would assure that the floors that are paid from the national treasury result in fair prices being paid to the producers.
This kind of situation does not apply to grain. A farmer may believe that the grade he receives is wrong. He has the right to send a sample to the board of grain commissioners which will give him the correct grade, and it is the obligation of the elevator 66968-9-2051
Supply-Agriculture
companies to buy the grain at the official grade set by the board. There should be some kind of tribunal or board to which farmers could send their eggs in cases of dispute for a proper and official grading. I am convinced that if this were available to the producer of eggs the companies that I suspect are undergrading eggs in many instances would give the producer an accurate grade.

What worries me about this particular point is that if it is considered to be legal by the Department of Justice then it will be left in the hands of the minister, the department and the board to decide on

Mr. Chairman, I shall try to be as brief as possible, but I do want to say a few words in connection with the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) at the close of last Friday's debate.
Speaking of agriculture in the province of Quebec in particular-since he was answering my questions-the Minister of Agriculture said:
If I may say a word with regard to this question of putting price supports under poultry, particularly broiler chicks in which, I think, the hon. member is particularly interested, I would point out that this is just not a practical possibility. I do not look upon the production of these broilers as a real farm operation, because it is really a factory operation. It does not require a farm. It does not require even a rural atmosphere. It can be carried on in the middle of a city. A man puts up a building, buys several thousand chicks and then feeds them up to three and a half pounds or so. Along those lines he can turn out birds by the thousand every week. It is not a farm operation at all; it is a production line operation, and because practically no ground is required it is the type of operation which can lead to almost unlimited production.

This statement by the Minister of Agriculture about the Canadian poultry industry, especially in eastern Canada since the broiler industry is centered chiefly in Ontario and Quebec, which accounts for more than 50 per cent of the whole Canadian production, -is illogical.
It was a bit of a shock to me to hear the Minister of Agriculture make such a statement, in the wake of what has been said by economists and people interested in Quebec farming. I was shocked, and that is why, in stating the case for Quebec farmers, I want to say that the poultry industry of that province, as indeed in Ontario, is a sector of family farm activity. If the Quebec poultry industry is destroyed, part of the farmers engaged in that industry will be wiped out.
On family farms, there are various types of production and poultry raising is a very valuable branch of it, because it can be left in the care of the farm youngsters or even the farmer's wife. However, under present conditions, it can be said that poultry raising has practically disappeared from family farms, because the trend is to integration. Protection is being afforded not to the farmers, but to integrators, as I said last week, and as the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has just said again today. However, Quebec farmers do not take the same view of the problem as the Minister of Agriculture. So on September 11, 1958, a farm delegation called on the minister to tell him of the plight of the poultry industry, and in its brief, it was stated that Canada had imported three million pounds of poultry from the United States, with a consequent drop in the price of poultry.
The brief further stated that the price of poultry, which was 24 cents a pound in June 1958, was down to 20 cents a pound in early September, because of larger imports of U.S. poultry. That was why farmers submitted a brief to the department, asking for greater protection for Canadian poultry producers and for a review of the customs tariff. In any case, the delegation recognized that it was difficult to change our customs tariff without inviting reprisals on the part of the United States. In the same brief, the farmers made the following suggestions to the hon. minister:
In the meantime, as an emergency measure, we would suggest that you place temporary restrictions on U.S. import of chicken, with a floor price

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is misinformed when he says that poultry raising is primarily a family farm business in Quebec. We had some survey made in connection with this business of raising poultry, particularly raising broilers, which is the big business as far as raising chickens is concerned at the present time. We discovered that something over 90 per cent of all these chickens produced are produced under controlled or integrated farming arrangements. That is the reason I have no intention whatever of putting a support under broiler chickens. Just about 90 per cent of the production is on a contract basis or a vertical integration basis. This is one industry in Canada in which vertical integration and contract farming combined have almost completely taken over the industry. There is therefore no justification, in my opinion, for a support price for these broiler chickens.
As far as the imports are concerned, they are so small in comparison to our total production that they could not possibly have any material effect on the price. The reason the price of broiler chickens, fowl and poultry generally is away down from what it was is that in spite of repeated warnings, the producers have produced far more than the market will absorb. The importation is down actually. The importation is not up on poultry of all kinds; it is down. In 1956 the importation of poultry from the United States amounted to 22 million pounds; in 1957 it was 12,270,000 pounds; in 1958 it was 12,045,000 pounds. It is true that the importation of broiler chickens last year was 6,102,000 pounds as compared with 1,313,000 pounds in 1957. However for other types of poultry the figures were down materially from those of the year before.
Therefore as to poultry imports on the whole-and you must take the whole picture; you just cannot take broiler chickens; you must take all the types of poultry which are dealt in or traded in-if you take them all together, as I say, imports from the United States are down in 1958 in comparison with those in 1957, and they are away down in comparison with those of 1956.
However, production in Canada has gone up terrifically, as I pointed out previously. The production of fowl of all kinds in 1957 was 279 million pounds. That was about twice as much as it had been about three years earlier. About three years earlier it was about half that figure. In 1958 it went up again from 279 million pounds to 346,861,000 pounds, an increase of 67 million pounds in the one year.

The worst of it is that this situation is continuing in 1959. I have the figures here to March 7 for 1958 and for 1959. In 1958 to March 7 production was 39,585,000 pounds, but to March 7 in 1959 it is 50,171,000 pounds. In other words production is just shooting up and up. If there were such a thing as a support price we would not have one tenth of the cold storage capacity required to hold the chickens that would be produced.
As I said last Friday, these things can be produced almost without limit. We have a terrific quantity of feed in this country. There is no limit, except the amount of available feed, on the amount of chickens that can be produced. If there were a guaranteed price which made the raising of them profitable, as I say, we would not have anything like the necessary cold storage facilities in which to hold what would be produced. It is the type of thing for which it is absolutely impossible to put in a support price. It is the very last thing in the world for which you can even contemplate putting one in.

the production of grain on the prairies into the production of increased quantities of livestock and livestock products. We will then have the agricultural producers outside of the prairies facing a crisis the like of which they have not seen at least since the early thirties.

It is essential now for the minister whose estimates we are considering and for other members of the cabinet to take a new and sympathetic look at the request of the farm delegation to improve prices for wheat, oats and barley on the prairies. The western grain producer, not because he wants to as a first choice but because he is being driven to it through low prices for grain, will turn to the production of meat and will place the agricultural industry in the rest of Canada in the direst peril.
If hon. members of this committee representing constituencies in Quebec and Ontario are prepared to see prairie producers go into the production of commodities other than grain at a much accelerated rate they are merely saying they are prepared to sacrifice the agricultural industry in their provinces. That is the great peril facing this nation, increasing agricultural production that is forcing down the prices of various farm commodities, with the grain producer going more and more into the production of livestock and livestock products, if no action is taken by the government at this time, thus putting the agricultural industry outside the prairies in even greater peril than it is in today.
I therefore make a plea to the Minister of Agriculture and the other members of the cabinet to reconsider their adamant position taken on previous occasions in respect of the request for deficiency payments on prairie wheat, oats and barley.

The understanding of the hon. member for Assiniboia concerning the reason for a great increase in the production of certain agricultural products is at fault. The fact that there is a great deal of grain in western Canada is not the reason; the increase stems from improvements in technological processes of all kinds, improvements in genetics and breeding and so forth. Because of the great improvements that have been made in breeds of animals of all sorts and breeds of seeds- hybrid com is a classic example-it has been possible to produce a great deal more than was the case 10, 15 or 25 years ago. This terrific increase in agricultural production is not characteristic only of Canada, but may be found in all highly developed countries of the world and is due essentially to improvement in methods, breeding and so on. As a result we are getting much bigger yields, as far as some products are concerned, than was the case before. We are getting fowl and livestock of all kinds which make more efficient use of their feed than was the case before; thus we can produce more cheaply as a result, and so on.

I do not want the statement just made by the minister to pass unchallenged. I agree immediately that there have been certain very definite improvements in techniques and that operators are able to handle larger units of production, all of which have resulted in increases in the rate of production.
I have not the statistics on my desk, but perhaps the minister's officials have, to show the very rapid increase in the production of cattle and hogs in the last couple of years. I do not think this is the result of any improvement in techniques at all. That has very little to do with it. The fact of the matter is that because of marketing conditions and because of prices, farmers said

Supply-Agriculture
that it they were going to stay in the business of farming at all they would have to produce cattle and hogs. There was no recent development in production techniques that encouraged this very rapid increase in the production of cattle and hogs. There have been improvements in the techniques of poultry production, but I do not think the minister himself would claim that the doubling and almost tripling, I think, in about four years in the production of poultry has to do, in the main, with any techniques that have developed within the last four years that were not available at any time immediately prior to four years ago.
1 know improved techniques have resulted in increased production, but the basic reason our producers are producing more cattle and hogs today is the fact that there are people on the prairies who are not able to make an adequate living in the production and marketing of grain, notwithstanding the statistics the minister has placed on the record, and they are now going into the production of hogs and cattle in a very large way.
I am sure the minister can get from his officials the increase in the population of cattle and hogs in the last two years, but I do not think he will say this tremendous increase is the result of any great improvement in techniques. The cow still gives birth to one calf a year on the average. If the rancher is able to do it there may be a few supplements he can feed to his calves to put on a few extra pounds of beef but certainly, as far as numbers are concerned, there is no great improvement in techniques which would lead me to believe that this is the reason for such tremendous increases. It is an economic reason, it is a price reason, and it is because the government has failed to do anything in response to the very strong requests which have been made by western grain producers.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock the minister and I were discussing a fishing

problem. I am sure the minister will recall that during last session he and I entered into a discussion of this same subject matter. I hope our discussion today will not result in the same sort of anger and difference of opinion that occurred last time. Up to approximately the middle of 1958 the subsidy paid by the Department of Agriculture toward the capital cost of cold storage facilities was limited to one-third of such cost. Some time around the middle of 1958 a further limitation was placed on the subsidy making it either one-third of the capital cost or $50,000, whichever was the lesser.
As I understood the reasons given by the minister he said that there was an abundance of cold storage facilities in Canada and that all we would be doing by retaining the one-third principle would be putting public money into the building of cold storage facilities when there was already an abundance and the facilities already in existence were not being used to anywhere near capacity. I believe the minister gave some figures indicating that use ranged as low as 50 per cent in a number of cases.
The objection I take to the application of the subsidy and to the change made last year is this. First, I do not think that the granting of subsidies to cold storage warehouses used for the storage of fish or fisheries products should come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture. If I may interpret the minister's remarks on the point of order he raised earlier, or perhaps misinterpret them as he may say later, I think that subconsciously he may feel that I have a valid point in this regard.
I attempted to get some information about the percentage of occupancy of existing cold storage facilities to determine whether, as the minister said, the percentage of occupancy was low and whether the low percentage of occupancy applied equally in the case of cold storage facilities for fisheries products and agricultural products. To that end I entered into correspondence with the minister and subsequently placed a question on the order paper which was answered on January 27. The answer appears on page 422 of Hansard and I should like to refer to the information contained therein. I inquired as to the number of cold storage warehouses used for fish products, the number used for agricultural products and so on. The answer given was that of the total number there were 249 warehouses that stored in the main fish and fisheries products; 1,969 storing in the main agricultural products; and another 850 classified as general and used for storing a variety of products.

I attempted to determine the percentage of occupancy of these various types of cold storage facilities and the answer I received, as found on page 422, was as follows:
The dominion bureau of statistics do not require cold storage warehouses to report what percentage of the space is occupied. They do require, however, a statement of the quantities of certain goods in storage and this information is published in various forms, many of which are on a monthly basis. The Department of Agriculture receives voluntary confidential reports showing the percentage occupancy of warehouses which represent about one-third of the total available refrigerated space in Canada.
The answer then proceeds to deal with the percentages I submit there is no indication that a differentiation is made between cold storage facilities for agricultural products and cold storage facilities for fisheries products. I certainly hope it is not the case but I am almost sure that where the number of such plants used for fisheries products is relatively minor numerically compared with the number used for agricultural products-the ratio is one to eight-the consideration given to the minor phase of the problem is not the type of consideration that probably should be given to it. I do not say that is the case in this instance but I rather suspect that fisheries products cold storage facilities were lumped together in the whole consideration of cold storage facilities when the decision was made to reduce the amount of the subsidy. The reason given was that there was too much space and it was not being used to the degree that it should be, and I suspect that the decision was based primarily on the total picture of cold storage warehouses and not on a break-down of the percentage of use for fisheries products and the percentage of use for agricultural products.

Whereas breeders of registered livestock consider ROP tests a necessity and,

Because of the results achieved through general co-operation to increase the yield of our dairy cattle as a result of proper selection based on official records of performance,
Be it resolved that the Quebec Ayrshire Breeders Association make strong representations to the Minister of Agriculture for Canada, following the decision not to increase the number of herds under ROP control.
Such a restriction has a paralysing effect first on the stock breeder who is a beginner and it curtails the results of the selective registry policy followed by our organization.
As a matter of fact, local farmers, more especially purebred livestock breeders, have been complaining over the past year that they cannot have control services for their dairy herds.
Today in the Bois Franc area there are at least 875 farmers organized into three livestock breeders clubs and two Holstein, Ayrshire livestock breeders clubs, including many purebred livestock breeders the importance of which is well established. Under the regulation governing registry, no bull can be certified or recognized by the association if the dam has not the ROP qualifications and is not classified according to its breed type. Such measure regarding restrictions to the registration stops automatically the whole plan designed to promote the production of purebred cattle.
This will eventually hurt the breeding stock markets.
There are in the constituencies of Drum-mond-Arthabaska and Megantic, and in most of the constituency of Lotbiniere, breeders' associations which are recognized as the best breeders of registered livestock in the province of Quebec.
Each year our breeders sell more than $400,000,000 worth of cross-bred and purebred stock for production and breeding purposes, such as dairy cows, stock heifers and bulls.
Furthermore, I would draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that the department of agriculture of the province of Quebec makes grants available for the exclusive purchase of certified bulls and heifers, out of certified dams. It is therefore essential to let the breeders freely control their production without any restrictions. In fact, for a few years now, Quebec experimental farms and agronomists have been doing a good deal of educational work aimed at improving cattle raising in my area. Many farmers have asked that inspection services be extended to their dairy herds, but unfortunately they were turned down by the department.
I think there is no sense in restricting those services after all the educational work designed to promote our livestock industry.

This statement which the hon. member has just made that applications for record of performance inspection are being refused because the department does not wish to extend the work is completely incorrect.

The actual fact of the matter is that there has been, on the part of farmers, a constantly increasing awareness of the value of these record of performance inspections and of getting their herds on record of performance. As a result there has been quite a rapid increase in the number of applications on the part of farmers to have their herds included. We just have not had sufficient staff to meet all these demands. We have asked for 20 new positions in order that we shall be able to extend the work and to take in the people who have now applied for it. The only way in which we can keep up with these applications is by increasing the number of the staff, and this we are in the process of doing.

I do not see why it should take so long to give satisfaction to our farmers. One case was brought to my attention of a farmer making an application last November. This was refused. In this connection the hon. member for Kootenay West will realize-*

-that I am in exactly the same position as one of the old racing parsons in England. I do not consider that I am involved in sin at all, through the fact that the department supervises race track betting. In fact, I consider the position to be just the reverse. The situation is that under the Criminal Code the Department of Agriculture is responsible for supervising parimutuel betting at race tracks, which is permitted by the Criminal Code. For that purpose we use the R.C.M.P. to supervise each race track when it is in operation. In Ottawa we have a small staff of three men who have general charge and supervision of race track betting operations and who give directions to the R.C.M.P. who attend at each track to collect the records and make sure we get our percentage of the gate, which is used in turn to pay for the supervision. The purpose is to ensure that the customer at the parimutuel plant gets a fair return on his bet; in other words, that there is no hanky-panky in connection with the parimutuel operation.
In addition, we carry out urinary and salivary tests on the horses to ensure that they have not been doped, thus, of course, changing what would otherwise be the odds in any race and the probability of a particular horse winning. We also operate the photo-finish equipment and what is called the eye in the sky in order to have a photographic record so that there can be no question as to which horse won a particular race. The percentage of the gate that we get is one-half of one per cent and the money so collected is used for these supervisory activities.

The minister did not indicate whether he gets any hot tips in this process and if he follows them up, but I take it from his remarks that there is a certain amount of income received. In effect the federal government gets a rake-off, somewhat like the house in a poker game. I am using these terms which are totally unfamiliar to me although I have heard them used before. What is the percentage of the take, how is it computed and what happens to the money? Does it go to the Department of Finance or the Department of National Revenue and is it then credited against the expenditures made by the Department of Agriculture? What is the relationship?

As I said a minute ago, we get one half of one per cent of the money

wagered. This money goes into the consolidated revenue fund and then the amount of money we expend has to be voted. That is the purpose of this vote. That is why we take a half of one per cent, so that the operation itself will pay for the supervision rather than the general taxpayers having to pay for it.

I am sure that the same general principle could be applied to quite a number of activities in which various government agencies are involved and whose purpose is to protect the general public. We get involved in protecting the public from the unscrupulous acts of certain individuals or corporations with respect to their pricing policies and so on and I wonder why the same principle could not be applied.

I think the hon. member has misunderstood. We have three people on the permanent staff here in Ottawa who have responsibility for the supervision of this race track betting. They keep the records and make sure that the general supervisory work is carried out. The actual work at each particular track is carried out by a mounted policeman. There are three people in the central office, and then they employ mounted policemen at each of the tracks during the time the race is being run. The mounted policeman who is doing this work in Calgary, for instance, is not the same one who does the work in Toronto.

Yes.
This would indicate that there is probably $100 million per year wagered at the race tracks.

I do want to say a word or two on this item because I have noticed, for the first time, that there is an amount for the federated women's institutes of Canada of $10,000. I must say that I am delighted to see this grant included in the estimates this year. I think I must say such a grant is long overdue for such a worthy organization. These women's institutes were commenced, I understand, at Stoney Creek in 1897. Provision was made for an organization of rural women to work for the welfare of rural women and the communities in which they live. I understand it followed the example set by the farmers' institute. It is very nice to know that on this occasion the ladies followed the example of the men.
I know that so far as my own district is concerned the women's institutes were established in 1909. My own mother was a very active person in the women's institutes in the interior of British Columbia. Since that time I have always taken a great interest in the work they have done and have admired the organization for making a tremendous contribution to the communities in which their activities take place.
Then in 1919 the federated women's institutes of Canada was established, which showed the continuing growth of the organization. I understand that today there are approximately 3,000 branches of the institute in Canada with approximately 100,000 members. The germ of the idea came from British
Supply-Agriculture
Columbia, and in 1937 the associated countrywomen of the world was organized, and of that international body the federated women's institutes of Canada are a constituent society. This great organization, which has not received too much publicity throughout the years in my opinion, has done more work with less money than any other organization in the country for the welfare of Canada as a whole. It has carried on, giving effect to its motto, "For Home and Country".
I know that in the early days this organization dealt with the questions of domestic science, home management and was active in local projects. In the communities in my area they look after cemeteries, local needs welfare of school children and things of that sort. They took the lead in working for equal rights for women. I am sure there are some members here from British Columbia who will remember the late Mrs. Ralph Smith who was very active in those days and who, with the support of the institute, obtained some improvement in the legislation in British Columbia which was of benefit to the women of that province. Since that time, their activities have widened. They are interested in national women's problems, problems that affect women in general.
Now they are greatly interested in international problems. I understand they are supporting the Food and Agricultural Organization, UNESCO and many other worthwhile organizations like that. I may tell you, Mr. Chairman, that I was never so pleased to support a vote as I am to support this one for $10,000 which is little enough for this magnificent organization of women in Canada.
I have witnessed how versatile they are. I remember very well what happened when one of the small communities in our district was threatened by forest fire and would possibly have been destroyed had it not been for the organization of women's institute in seeing that the tools were provided and taken to the fire guards and that refreshments were provided over a day or so that the men could continue to fight the fire. It was a very close squeak but finally this community in question was saved as a result of the organization and co-operation of the women's institute.
I can tell you something else, and I must not take long in doing so. However, this vote arouses my interest and my support. As you may know, the women's institute in my district was the first organization in Canada, as far as I know, to establish midwifery by telephone. I remember an isolated rancher whose wife was going to have a child miles away from anywhere. His wife told him to phone the women's institute. They got in touch with an elderly member of the

women's institute at the other end of the telephone miles away and she instructed the husband what to do. That new Canadian was born and is now a resident of my district and possibly he votes for me. In any event, I just give these as two illustrations of the value of the work of the women's institutes in the local field. I could go on at great length, with these early stories of the women's institutes but I do not wish to detain the committee. However, in conclusion I want to say that I am sure all members of this committee will give whole hearted support to this small grant of $10,000 to this organization which has done so much for Canada since 1897.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to rise on item 23 but you passed over it very quickly. I want to ask a question in connection with item No. 23. I should like to ask the reason for the reduction in the grant to the royal winter fair in Toronto. Was it for some special event last year? What is the usual grant to the royal winter fair?

The only reason for the reduction is that the royal winter fair have not yet completed their plans. They informed us that they did not think they would be able to do more than spend upwards of $15,000 on the preparation of plans and so forth as far as this year was concerned. Therefore, in order to avoid having in the estimates an item of a quarter of a million dollars, which was in last year but was not used-and which was just unnecessarily padding the estimates and gave to the committee actually an improper picture-this amount was put in. I asked the royal winter fair people how much they were actually going to spend. They said this would probably be the amount, and that is the amount I put in rather than a quarter of a million dollars.
Is there any other grant made to the royal winter fair?
An annual grant of $50,000 is made but this is part of a special grant which was given to the royal winter fair some considerable time ago and which they have not yet taken up.
Would it get more if it needed it later on?

This grant is in order to improve their livestock facilities at Toronto. They were given a total grant of $1 million. They have not yet expended this money. They expected last year to spend about a quarter of a million dollars. That is why $250,000 was put into the estimates last year. But then they ran into difficulty, I think because of the new extension of the Queen Elizabeth way or the four-lane highway which

is to go into Toronto in that area. This four-lane highway took up some of the land, as I understand it, on which they were going to construct these new buildings. Therefore they were obliged to cancel those plans and are in the process of making new ones now. That is the reason for the hold-up.

The minister would perhaps wish to deal with the question put by the hon. member for Welland. The royal winter fair is one of the great institutions of its kind, not only in Ontario but, I suppose, in the world. If the directors of the royal winter fair felt that the moneys now appropriated were insufficient for their purposes I take it from the question-although I am not clear from the answer- that more moneys would be appropriated by way of a special supplementary estimate later on.

As I say, the agreement was made to provide them with $1 million to extend their facilities. As the hon. member says, this is the big winter fair in Canada. It is the showplace of Canadian agriculture in Canada. On that account it was made this special grant. I do not think the directors of the royal winter fair are going to need more than the amount that is in the estimates this year. That is why this amount is in rather than the greater amount.

I could not possibly let this opportunity pass without saying just a word agreeing in part at least with the hon. member for Kootenay West. It is not often that I can agree with what he says, but on this occasion I certainly can do so with regard to the federated women's institutes of Canada and this grant to them of $10,000. I am sure it is not the first time, however, that this grant has been given. On a previous occasion I am sure this same grant was made to the women's institutes of Canada. I believe that was on the occasion of the meeting here some few years ago of the federated women's institutes of the world. In addition, I want to point out that while the first women's institute was formed at Stoney Creek, I have the honour to have in my constituency the birthplace of the lady who started this institution, namely Adelaide Hunter Hoodless. It is situated within a mile and one-half of my own home at St. George, Ontario. I should like to add that the site of her birthplace is being marked this year by the archaeological and historical sites board of the province of Ontario. It will be quite an occasion. I think it is to be held on June 12.

I think perhaps I had better just say that I was glad to put in this grant

for the women's institutes and get it accepted as a regular grant amongst these other grants in this department. This is the first time that this has been the case. The women's institutes received a special grant on the occasion mentioned by the hon. member some years ago. But this is the first time that they have ever been put in for a regular grant, although they have been asking for this grant for many years. I was extremely glad finally to succeed in getting this institution accepted as one which should have an annual grant.

I should like to know whether there are in the country other organizations which have applied for grants and if so, whether their requests were refused? Are these grants which are listed on page 112 fixed annual grants or are they determined by the minister or by his officials or on the recommendation of the officials to the minister?

They are not fixed. They can be changed annually. In most cases they have been arrived at as a result of discussions with the organization concerned and a determination made of what appeared to be a reasonable sort of grant for the dominion government to make to the particular institution concerned. As I said, the women's institutes have now been asking for many years for an annual grant and it was always refused. Eventually I managed to get the treasury board to agree that this was the type of institution which should have a grant under this particular item. That is why the $10,000 is in for that particular institution. As to what other institutions may have asked for grants and been refused, I do not know. I cannot recall any that have been refused since I have been Minister of Agriculture but I have no doubt that over the years there have been organizations which asked for grants and did not get them.
I should like to ask the minister, in connection with this grant of $50,000 to the Canadian national livestock records, where these records are kept. Are they kept here in Ottawa?
Yes, they are kept here in Ottawa in the Canadian national livestock record office. It is on Queen street.
Is that for the whole of Canada?
Yes, that is for all Canada, and we make a grant toward the carrying on of this work.

27. Freight assistance on western feed grains,
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief remarks on this item with regard to the distribution of animal feeds in the province of Quebec, and particularly in the Sorel district. In fact, farmers in this district are complaining that they can no longer purchase grain from elevators located in Sorel. I think the owners of these elevators

are more interested in handling grain for transshipment purposes than for delivery to farmers.
Some ten constituencies north and south of the St. Lawrence river are entirely dependent on grain elevators in Sorel for their supplies. Last year, farmers had a hard time getting even small quantities of grain from these elevators. This has caused hardship to livestock breeders in the district, because that is where the farmers can get the cheapest grain, taking transportation costs into account.
I therefore ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) whether the North American Elevator Company Limited, which owns these elevators, is authorized to deliver grain to farmers in the Sorel area, and if not, I should like to know why.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I am not clear as to what the situation is about which the hon. member complains. This item, however, covers the subsidy we pay on the movement of grain from the western provinces down east or to British Columbia. The question of whether a particular elevator will or will not deliver grain at a farmer's farm does not come under this item at all nor indeed is it a matter within the purview of the Department of Agriculture. We have nothing to do with whether a particular concern delivers grain to a farmer's farm. I should think that would be entirely governed by the law of the province or perhaps it would be a business decision of the company concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two questions in respect of this item under which we are asked to vote $20 million for freight assistance on feed grain. At this time I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a few matters of importance to my area. I have in my hand a fairly recent communication from the Department of Agriculture a portion of which I should like to place on the record:
As you know, when we agreed to pay freight assistance on movement out of the British Colum-bia-Peace River block into other areas of British Columbia, this was the first time we had paid assistance on movement in a province. We did have some reservations about opening up this precedent, but felt that it was completely illogical to pay freight assistance on British Columbia-Peace River grain if it moved via Alberta but not if it moved directly. The British Columbia-Peace River block has always been a part of the western grain-producing area for the purpose of our freight assistance regulations, and therefore we undertook to pay on direct movement over the Pacific Great Eastern.
Supply-Agriculture
The Creston-Wynndel area has never been a part of the western grain-producing area for the purpose of our freight assistance regulations, although I realize that it is a designated area under the wheat board.
At the present time the area in which t I live is producing one-half a million bushels of wheat annually. In the over-all picture of Canadian wheat production that is not very large but it is considerable in relation to the output of this area. We are having considerable difficulty in getting our wheat to market due to our geographic location and because of various toll bridges and, incidentally, the fact that we do not have the trans-Canada highway. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention that had the trans-Canada highway been put through the southern section of the province I believe many of our problems would have been removed. Last autumn a news story appeared in local newspapers which caused considerable interest. The press release read:
British Columbia grain growers will get a federal freight subsidy on feeds shipped to other British Columbia farmers from Peace River and Creston areas.
At present freight rates, the assistance will be $7.90 a ton from Peace River points, $5.90 from Creston.
This compares with $6.50 from Calgary and $7.90 from Edmonton, the maximum.
This news item was later refuted by the department. I would request that some consideration be given to the agricultural problems of our area. Not very long ago we had to have a permit before feed grains could be shipped out of our area to coastal markets which involved delay, but thanks to the minister and his department this problem has now been resolved satisfactorily and through their co-operation we are now able to get permits practically on a moment's notice.
A major cause of concern in the constituency of Kootenay East is that we experience difficulty in getting our wheat into the Vancouver market. At the present time a certain degree of discrimination exists against this area of British Columbia. If the assistance referred to in this estimate is to apply to feed grains anywhere in Canada then my area should receive some consideration.

Mr. Chairman, this subsidy for the movement of feed grains is for interprovincial movements and not for movements within a province. That is the reason why the subsidy is not paid on the movement of grain from Creston or Wynndel to other points in British Columbia. Any grain moved from Creston to Ontario would be eligible for assistance. We do not, however, pay the subsidy on wheat moving between Creston and the Okanagan valley or from

Supply-Agriculture
Kootenay East to Kootenay West which is not very far away. If we did so, the entire subsidy system in respect to the movement of feed grains would have to be completely changed.
At the present time we have received complaints from the corn growers in Ontario over the fact that this subsidy is paid. Some people in Ontario want this subsidy abolished because it puts them at a disadvantage so far as the sale of their corn, wheat or other grains is concerned.
Does the minister agree with the submission made by the corn growers?

No, I do not. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and all agricultural organizations except those representing solely wheat and corn growers have pressed us to keep this subsidy in operation. If you started to pay a subsidy within a province it would mean you would be saying, in effect, "We will pay the charges on all movements of grain for feeding purposes."
Mr. Chairman, would the minister be good enough to answer one question. Can an eastern farmer purchase grain direct from the wheat board or does he have to purchase from a wheat concern?
As long as he takes a carload he can get it direct from the wheat board; but, of course, the wheat board does not sell except in carload lots.
Is that quite correct? The wheat board always has an agent through which they sell.
Yes, technically.
I think there is an intermediary; it cannot be made out to the wheat board as such.
That is correct.

31.	Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $5,153,000.

As the minister knows, he has had repeated requests for years for an amendment to this act to make it apply on a statutory basis to all provinces in Canada. A great deal of interest is taken in this question in British Columbia because the good work which is being done under the act in the prairie provinces and, to a limited extent, I understand, by estimates in other provinces but not by statute, is generally recognized. Can the minister inform the committee whether the government is giving consideration to widening the application of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all provinces in Canada so that they will enjoy the same opportunities?

Before the minister answers I would like to add my voice to what has been said by the hon. member. I know we do have several projects going on which are carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. As the hon. member says, these are being carried on under special provisions of the act. If the act were amended to include all of the provinces a great deal of good could be done in British Columbia. You could also change the name of the act from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to "Western Farm Assistance Act", or something along that line.

I should like to say a few words to the Minister of Agriculture. I hope that he can extend the jurisdiction of the act. Because of the way the act is constituted at the present time some of the areas

in my constituency are not covered. This, of course, presents quite a problem to some of the people because there is a considerable amount of diversification going on and many of these people depend on dugouts for their water supply. If they are to diversify they must have water. In some areas certain portions of the municipalities are not covered. This creates a difficulty for the people within the boundaries of a particular municipality.
In addition, I might suggest to the minister that the present rate of compensation paid should be increased. The original intent was to compensate for part of the construction of dugouts and dams. Since then the cost of construction has gone up considerably. Perhaps the time has come when we should take another look at this, and a higher rate of compensation be paid.

Mr. Chairman, as far as the last point is concerned, we increased the rate of help given for dugouts, small irrigation projects and so forth, effective April 1 of this year. At the present time the amount of assistance available for a dugout is $250 rather than $125 which had existed; $300 for one of the small dams in place of $150; and $600 for an irrigation project in place of the $350 which had prevailed before. In other words, the scale of assistance has been practically doubled. As far as dugouts and dams are concerned it was doubled. For the other it was almost doubled. For larger excavations we pay up to seven cents a yard for excavation work in place of the four and one-half cents which had prevailed before.
Now, as far as extending the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all parts of Canada is concerned, to begin with I think perhaps I had better point out that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was brought into existence to do exactly as the act says, namely to rehabilitate certain areas in western Canada, the dry areas of the southern prairies. The provisions of the act were limited^ to those drier areas. That is why there is the line of demarcation in the western provinces. The areas south of that line are eligible for P.F.R.A. work and benefits, and the areas north of it are not. There has been, of course, constant pressure on to extend that line northwards, and there has been some justification, I think, in certain areas particularly for extending it northwards because drier conditions began to prevail in some areas where they had not prevailed previously. Therefore, there has been some extension of the line northwards.
The work which has been carried on in British Columbia was not carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; it was carried on under special votes appearing in
Supply-Agriculture
the estimates from time to time. However, it was done by the P.F.R.A. personnel, but it was not part of the prairie farm rehabilitation activities actually or strictly speaking.
Now, as hon. members know, we have a study going on, on a project to put into effect a national soil and water conservation program. We had a conference on this with representatives from all the provinces a few months ago, and it was decided at that conference that this was a thing which would take a considerable amount of preparation in order to get down to anything which would be practical and workable. As a result, it was decided to hold a full-scale conference in 1960. In the meantime, the provincial and dominion officials concerned -it carries over into several departments in both the dominion government on the one hand and the provincial governments on the other-would make the necessary research and preparatory work. As a result of that conference I hope we shall be able to bring into being something in the nature of what you might call a national soil and water authority or organization, which probably would then absorb the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act program as part of its activities. I think that is the way in which the things will move rather than to expand the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act into other provinces.

I was very interested in hearing the minister's explanation when replying to the requests of various members for the extension of the application of the act to all provinces. The minister knows that in my constituency there is a district known as the Slocan valley which has been somewhat depopulated because of certain tendencies on the part of some of the citizens of the district that are not very well appreciated by the other section of the community. Consequently the valley is not producing what it was even 40 years ago.
At the request of the Slocan valley agricultural development association I wrote the minister asking if the federal government would undertake surveys of the acreage, soil, suitability of the soil for certain crops and so on in the valley and the minister replied that favourable consideration would be given to such a request if an application or representations were made by the government of British Columbia. Should that occur, could that sort of thing be undertaken even prior to the development of the legislation the minister has just mentioned?

It could only be undertaken if it were covered by a special vote in the estimates. If the hon. member will look at the estimates he will see one or two special

Supply-Agriculture
votes. There is a special vote of $150,000 for diking and cutoffs in respect of the Assini-boine and Qu'Appelle rivers. Under the vote for major irrigation and reclamation projects certain projects are named which can be covered in this way but they do not come under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. In the same way supervision of the building of the South Saskatchewan dam is being carried on by personnel of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act administration but as far as the cost and legislative authority are concerned they are covered by the vote for major irrigation projects.

I have a very brief comment having to do with the statement the minister has just made that the amount for which a farmer may be eligible with respect to the construction of a dugout has been increased from $125 to $250. I want to thank the minister because in my opinion this is a very timely move. I think such action should have taken place long ago. I am not holding the minister responsible for the fact that it was not taken long ago because the amount of $125 is the sum that has been paid for many years under a former administration.
With conditions on the prairies extremely dry at the present time and with the development of a very substantial livestock industry, the provision of water becomes a greater and greater problem. Beyond question the agricultural producers on the prairies will welcome the statement of the minister with regard to the increase in the amount that a farmer may receive when a dugout or small dam is constructed. In my opinion what the government has now done is to take into account the very great increase in excavation costs over the years. In view of the increased costs and in view of the great necessity of adequate water supplies, unquestionably this is an essential increase.

I should like to ask the minister a question regarding the construction of dugouts adjacent to populated localities. As he probably knows, in my area extensive use has been made of P.F.R.A. facilities and I think quite a bit of flexibility has been apparent. I am wondering whether there has been any change of policy during the last couple of years regarding the construction of dugouts in areas such as I have mentioned.

As far as I have been concerned in administering the act I have had regard to the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which lays down very definitely that money expended for dugouts or other purposes under the act must be for the benefit and advantage of agriculture. Wherever it was established that a dugout

or a small dam was going to be for the advantage of agriculture in a particular area and was justified on agricultural grounds I have been quite ready to go ahead and authorize its construction in so far as we have had personnel and money available for the purpose. However, I have had a very large number of requests from towns and villages throughout western Canada to construct town water supply systems, in some cases even sewage systems, and in every case I have refused because projects of that sort are not covered by the act and I have no authority under the legislation to expend the taxpayers' money for these purposes.
