32.	Major irrigation and reclamation projects in the western provinces, including payments in respect of the South Saskatchewan river project to be made in accordance with the agreement that was entered into between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Saskatchewan on the 25th day of July, 1958, $14,649,128.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on item 32 which pertains to irrigation and reclamation I should like to be permitted to relate to the house some of the observations I made and impressions I gained last summer when I visited the Taber district of Alberta. Much irrigation has been done in this district. On the day in question a rare opportunity presented itself to me when, on the kind invitation of the district engineer, Mr. Ellaf Olofson, I joined a group of P.F.R.A. engineers and technicians in a tour of inspection of irrigation projects and testing plots. This, I understand, is done about once a month in order to provide P.F.R.A. personnel with an opportunity to familiarize themselves with some of the new methods and latest discoveries in the field of irrigation and reclamation.
I found the tour most interesting and very informative. Although I am a dry land farmer myself, the short inspection tour convinced me of the merits of irrigation and the benefits a farmer can derive from the use of water. One outstanding example was the farm of a young American who had only come to Alberta in 1957. He came originally from a place in the United States where much irrigation is practised, and that is one reason why he wanted to settle in a district in Alberta where irrigation is carried on at the present time. The other reason was the price he would have had to pay for irrigated land in the United States. Here he could buy the same amount of land for about one-tenth of the price he would have had to pay in the United States.
From what I could see this farmer knew irrigation inside out and his first crop last

year justifies my statement. He pointed out to us that he had not had enough time to put irrigation to work by growing row crops such as sugar beets and so he had had to be content to grow flax in his first year. The day we were there he was harvesting his flax and according to his estimate it was running about 35 bushels to the acre. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that at present the price of flax is about $3 a bushel. I must say I have never seen a better crop or better sample of flax anywhere.
He told us that he only irrigated his land twice during the year, but the outstanding feature was the method he had applied. It is the so-called corrugated irrigation method which is supposed to be the least expensive and one that requires little labour. If I may be permitted, I should like to try to describe to you this corrugated irrigation process.
The land to be sown to crop is prepared in the usual manner up to the point where it is ready for the drill. Then, the whole field is corrugated with an implement that looks very much like a rod weeder except that there is no rod. There is one row of stiff cultivator shanks spaced about 30 inches apart, instead of rods. There are 8-inch shovels attached to these shanks, and these shovels look very much like miniature irrigation ditchers. This is the implement that is used to ditch the field. This process leaves the whole surface of the field marked with little ditches about eight inches wide, three to four inches deep and, of course, 30 inches apart. The farmer then sows his crop in the ordinary way, running in the same direction as the ditches. One would think that while irrigating a corrugated field some seeds in these ditches would be washed out or drowned. However, from what I could observe there appeared to be just as many stalks in the ditches as in other parts of the fields.
The other place to which we were taken during this tour was a livestock farm or what we would call a cattle feed lot. It, too, was an irrigated farm but instead of having cattle grazing in a pasture the procedure is reversed and the grass is brought to the feed lot for the cattle. The pasture is divided into a number of parcels of equal size. These parcels are used in a revolving order. When the grass is high enough in the first parcel, it is cut and loaded into trucks, all in one operation, and taken to these feed lots. After the grass has been taken off a parcel, the field is irrigated and fertilized if this is required. Then, the operation is moved to the second parcel. This method of pasturing cattle, which is called mechanical grazing, is very economical. Much less land is required and the land can
Supply-Agriculture
be irrigated and fertilized whenever that is needed. If ordinary pasturing practices were followed this would not be possible because the cattle would be allowed to roam around in the fields. The feeder cattle make much more rapid weight gains and in much less time. All this means a great saving to the farmer in time and money.
In conclusion, I should like to say that in my opinion the P.F.R.A. with its competent staff of engineers and technicians, has done a commendable job in the field of irrigation and reclamation, as well as in other fields. As a result of all this, farmers who can apply themselves to irrigation farming can do this more economically now as a result of the research experience which is passed on to them. It is my firm belief that irrigation should be extended wherever this is possible in Canada. It is an investment in the future of Canada's agriculture.
I wonder if the minister would give the committee a summary of the work done to date in respect of the South Saskatchewan river project?

Mr. Chairman, by the end of last year we had let six contracts. One of them was for an access road; one was for the substructure for a construction bridge; one was for an abutment on one side of the river, a big earth-moving job; one was for the construction of administrative headquarters for the P.F.R.A. personnel who will be supervising this job. The construction area was provided with sewers, water and so forth so that it could be used by the construction companies in establishing their camps, and so on.
Since that time, we have given out two other contracts. One contract is for the processing of the aggregate, and this was a contract for $812,000. This is to get the aggregate mixture, the crushed stone, gravel and so forth, ready for the concrete work. Another contract was for the construction of a north access road, that is coming in from the north. The first access road was to come in from the east. Those are the contracts that have been let to date. There will be a number of other contracts let during the next month or two months.
What is the estimated amount of the contracts for the access roads?
For the access roads; the first one was $172,469; that was the east access road.
Was that included in the first six contracts?
Yes.

There are now eight contracts?

Supply-Agriculture
Yes, with an aggregate of $5.5 million.

I noticed in the estimates, page 122, there is provision for $8.61 million, which is the estimated expenditure for the South Saskatchewan river development project. Is that the total amount for the fiscal year or is there another amount included in this item on page 123?
No, that is the estimated amount which we will expend during this fiscal year.

The progress that is being made toward the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam, and the general project, is most welcome. I think the people of Saskatchewan are pleased that this project will, in due course, be completed. I am certain history will show that it was one of the far-sighted policies that has been proceeded with on a joint, co-operative basis between the Saskatchewan government and the federal government. While it was necessary for the federal government to agree before construction could take place, the position of the Saskatchewan government for many years has been that this is a worth-while project and should have been proceeded with long ago. Therefore, because of the co-operative attitude of both governments this project is now under way.
I have a question I should like to raise, Mr. Chairman, in connection with this project. I believe the Minister of Agriculture is very familiar with this general question. I refer to the wage rates that will be paid to workers performing services on that project. Most of the workers involved, no doubt, will be working for the contractors, but there is concern amongst the labouring groups that the wages paid on the South Saskatchewan project will not conform to the general wage rates paid similar labour in Saskatchewan.

I wonder if the hon. member would allow me to say that the matter of wage rates is handled by the Department of Labour, therefore, I think the time for him to ask these questions is on the estimates of the Department of Labour which follow immediately after the Department of Agriculture. I have had nothing to do with the matter of wage rates. It has been handled by the Department of Labour.

So far as I am concerned, I do not wish to delay the passage of these estimates beyond today. I do know a great deal of the correspondence in regard to this question has come to the Minister of Agriculture. I am quite prepared to discuss it at a later stage with the Minister of Labour.
I referred all the letters to the Minister of Labour.

I hope the Minister of Labour has taken action in this regard, and that the wages that are paid by contractors will not be low wages, nor will they be the lower wages that are general in the area where the dam is to be constructed.
As hon. members can well realize, the wages that are usually paid in outlying communities are lower than the wages that are paid in the larger urban communities. There will be a great many workers attached to this project. I shall accept the minister's advice. I shall take the matter up with the Minister of Labour when his estimates are before the house. I hope that I can get a satisfactory answer from him. I should be quite happy to have him give us the information now. Certainly this is a situation that requires action by the government.

In the details on page 122 I notice that there are two listings which are rather hard to follow. For instance, about half way down the page there is listed "Lil-looet river reclamation (Pemberton)". I imagine that is the Pemberton valley in British Columbia. It is under item (13) or one of the items under (13) and it is listed at $150,000. Then right following that, under the heading "Further details for major irrigation and reclamation projects in the western provinces" we again find listed "Lillooet river reclamation (Pemberton), $150,000". By looking quickly at these details, it would appear to me that all of the items listed in one section are just re-listed again farther down.
It is just a different type of breakdown for the convenience of hon. members.
So that they will be able to see the actual projects?
Yes.
There are two in British Columbia. One is the Lillooet river reclamation (Pemberton) and the other one is the British Columbia fruit lands irrigation.

Item agreed to.
36. Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration, $630,069.

On item 36 dealing with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act I should like to bring to the attention of the committee a request that was sent to the Minister of Agriculture some time ago by Mr. Harry Riviere, who is secretary of the rural municipality of Brokenshell, at Trossachs. His suggestion to the minister was an excellent one, I thought. It had to do with the practice of the office

of the prairie farm assistance officials. He made the point to the minister that when an area has been surveyed as to whether or not it will be eligible for prairie farm assistance, the result of that survey should be made available to each farmer who has signed a crop report but is subsequently declared ineligible for payment. He points out-and I think from my own experience I can agree with him wholeheartedly-that in a given area that has been inspected, a farmer who has signed a crop report and hopes he will be eligible for prairie farm assistance but who is subsequently found under the act to be ineligible, does not find this out by any direct communication from the office but merely hears it very often from some of his neighbours who are eligible and who receive cheques. Then the farmers who have been shut out under the provisions of the act immediately begin writing to the office criticizing the department and asked for reinspection and so on. His suggestion was that there should be a short note sent out. It could be a mimeographed note, probably, that could be used as a standard thing. There might have to be a number of various forms but it certainly would not have to be a new letter in each case. His suggestion was that producers who have had their crops inspected or their yields inspected should be notified when they are ineligible for payment.
I know the minister has had that letter among the many letters he receives. I do not know whether he has given it any further consideration since he has received it. However, to my mind it was a constructive suggestion. There may be some obvious objection to that kind of practice; I would not know. However, I certainly feel that it is something that should be given sympathetic consideration.

I gave consideration to it. I made some inquiries as to how many letters this procedure would involve. I think it ran to somewhere between 100,000 and 150,000 letters. Of course, the administrative cost of this procedure would be considerable. It is a thing which I think we might handle by sending letters out only to the people in a particular municipality who are not paid.

Oh, yes; that is right. There is no need to send a letter to a man who is going to be paid. He gets his cheque and a little note with it, which was the practice initiated by the previous administration so that the provincial government would not get any credit for it and that is perfectly understandable. He gets a little note saying, "This payment comes to you from the federal government". I have no objection to that procedure. We might as well keep our people as well informed as we 66968-9-207
Supply-Agriculture
can. Certainly there would be no need to send a letter to people who are getting a cheque. The cheque itself is information enough for people who are eligible. But for those who are ineligible-
As a result of your speech, the minister would like to send cheques to everybody.

I should be happy to see that but I am not nearly as optimistic as is my friend the hon. member for Essex East. But in fairness to the Minister of Agriculture, may I say this, and it is nice to end a discussion of the estimates of the department on a kindly note. I can say without fear of successful contradiction that the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in recent months has shown a great improvement over its administration in former years. If the Leader of the Opposition says that that is not a friendly note, if he would check with the farmers who have been receiving cheques he would find that they consider it a friendly thing and a correct thing because certain amendments that were brought into the act on a previous occasion have made it possible for more producers who have crop failures and are entitled to benefit under the act to receive payment.
Would the hon. member not agree that the administration under Mr. Gardiner perhaps has never been excelled?
I do not agree with that statement. I would say it has never been excelled as a political machine.
Oh, oh.

In other respects, it has been excelled. After this government has been in office for a few years-and we hope it is not too long- they may have learned some of the tricks that the former minister of agriculture used to use.
I want to say to the minister that if he would accept my suggestion he would get less criticism of his department. The farmers today are pleased that more of them- although not as many as they would wish because the matter is still not on an individual basis-who have a crop failure are in fact able to get payment.
I have just one point to make.
Oh, no.
Five o'clock.

There is one small point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman. There are farmers who have permit books and who are paying in under P.F.A.A. but they will never

Private Bills
be eligible for payment under P.F.A.A. because they could never be included in a six-section group. They have made representations to me that they think it would be only fair that, if they were not eligible for payment, their payment books should be marked specially so that they will not be obliged to make payment or so that they can get reimbursement. It is impossible for them to benefit under this act and they should like to be removed from the paying end.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: EXPORT FINANCE CORPORATION OF CANADA LIMITED
EXPORT FINANCE CORPORATION OF CANADA LIMITED
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-17, to incorporate Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to incorporate a company under the name of the Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited. The objects of the corporation would be to finance the exchange of commodities between Canada and other nations of the world, and to facilitate the overseas trade of Canada by extending credit for the export of various agricultural and manufactured products.
The general lending policy of the corporation would be two-fold: first, assistance to Canadian companies and exporters in financing exports of these products which I have mentioned and, second, the provision of loans to foreign governments, corporations and importers for financing the purchase of Canadian materials, equipment and services as they are required in the development of industry and natural resources abroad.

Applicants for loans would be required to show a good credit standing, and in addition the assured ability to obtain the dollar exchange necessary to service the loan. Loans would be made only for specific purposes, that is, loan commitments would be entered into only upon the borrower providing ample evidence that the proceeds would be used for the purchase of Canadian products, goods or services.
Most of the important exporting countries of the world are assisted in their export trade by similar lending agencies either governmental or private. Since Canada has in recent years become increasingly dependent on her export trade, it is most important that our export business be given every encouragement in the increasingly competitive world markets. The corporation will provide financing facilities such as have been available in England through various merchant guilds that have operated in that country for many decades and which contributed so much toward making England one of the world's great trading nations.
This particular field of export financing is normally beyond the scope of the Canadian chartered banks because it presumes the granting of credits on a much more extended basis than that exercised by the banks. The corporation's services are intended to complement but not compete with those presently offered by the chartered banks. While it is intended that the corporation will enter all aspects of export-import financing, including the granting of long term credit, it will not entertain any type of financing obtainable from a chartered bank in Canada.
The chartered banks have not wanted to make long term loans of this nature because there is no agency presently operating in Canada where the banks could discount these loans. Perhaps it is not generally recognized that while the federal government will insure credit extended to foreign buyers it does not provide the credit. The establishment of a financing agency such as is proposed in this bill which will trade in these credits as well as providing them should meet a definite need in Canada for the continued development of her export market in agricultural and manufactured products.
It is contemplated that the corporation would entertain proper loans for sums as low as $500. It is not proposed that a maximum figure should be established and should any single transaction or series of transactions call for a higher amount of financing than the corporation is willing to entertain it might form a financing syndicate with other lenders in order that the total financial assistance required could be furnished.

It is not anticipated that instalment financing would mature in a period any greater than five years. However, the corporation would be willing to participate with others ready to accept maturities for longer periods. With regard to the financing of projects or developments, maturities might extend up as far as 20 years. The interest rates to be charged by the corporation would vary from transaction to transaction and from country to country depending on the financial terms, the credit of the borrower and the guarantees furnished.
It is proposed that the corporation would have a capitalization of $50 million represented by 10 million shares of the par value of $5 each and it appears at the present time that some of the chartered banks of Canada, if not all of such banks, will be subscribers to the capital of the corporation. I have also been advised that when the capital stock of the corporation is offered for sale the public will be given the opportunity to subscribe and take up the remainder of any such offering.
The bill, of course, will be referred to the appropriate committee where hon. members will have ample opportunity to discuss it fully with its sponsors who will sit in with committee members to give a full explanation with respect to each clause and answer any and all questions in regard to the general policy of the corporation. The chairman of the standing committee on banking and commerce of the other place, had the following remarks to make with regard to the testimony of the witnesses that appeared before the committee:
We had before us in the committee representatives of several banks. I particularly recall Mr. E. Ernst, assistant general manager of the Bank of Montreal, who said that in his view this bill was sound in principle and would fill a gap in our financing of exports. He thought it would be of great value to Canadian industry. Mr. Arthur Mayne, associate general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada, supported that view. Mr. K. W. Taylor, deputy minister of finance, indicated to the committee that there was a definite field for the kind of thing contemplated in this bill and which does not now exist in financing in Canada. Mr. Hugh Aitken, president of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, was very strong in his statement as to the purpose which a company of this kind could serve. He indicated there would be no conflict between the operations of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation and this new corporation, if and when it is incorporated.
The chairman of the committee then went on to say:
In the course of our consideration of the bill in committee, we had before us not only these bankers and other men I have already mentioned, but also a Mr. Stanger, who was one of the promoters of the bill. We also had Mr. Hurter, the head of a very large engineering firm with engineering operations in various parts of the world,

Export Finance Corporation who was able to cite chapter and verse from contracts and tenders that had been invited from various parts of the world, this year, last year and the year before. The nature of the capital goods required was such that Canada could have been in the competitive market, but the terms presented difficulties. For instance, Egypt wanted five years' credit in relation to certain capital goods, and although some manufacturers in Canada considered the invitation tender, not one was in a position to take on the job, because not one could get the financing. X say this corporation is intended to fill that need. Whether it will do so completely, or at all, will depend upon how skillfully it is operated once it is incorporated and gets going.
After having read the report of the committee, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate that body on the excellent job they did in scrutinizing this bill and for the suggestions they made that formed the basis of the amendments that brought this bill up to the excellent standard and form in which it is now presented to this house.

maintopic: EXPORT FINANCE CORPORATION OF CANADA LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few brief comments in seconding this motion. The company which seeks incorporation will fulfil a very great need that exists at the present time in respect to the field of foreign exports. Many of our Canadian companies have been under a great handicap in competing for foreign trade because many of the foreign purchasers, like our local consumers, are purchasing on credit and although the Export Credits Insurance Corporation has been of great assistance in guaranteeing the credit to other companies it has not assisted our companies by being able to turn their sales into cash and thus enabling them to continue the financing of further business. Therefore, this company will fulfil a need which, as the sponsor said, the commercial banks are not able to do.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that this company will be able to purchase or discount foreign trade papers which are received by Canadian companies in their selling of goods, and it will also be able to give credit assistance to foreign buyers of goods and services. I think we see here a very definite note running through the whole bill of emphasis on assisting those who wish to buy Canadian goods or set up companies in other countries using Canadian materials. I understand that at the present time there are such countries as Ceylon, Ethiopia, India, Iraq, Pakistan, South Africa, Indonesia, Malaya, Egypt, Uruguay requesting certain capital and consumer goods, and they wish to buy those on credit. They cannot do so in Canada. Our companies cannot sell to those countries under the present international arrangement,

as far as credit is concerned, with our own banking facilities. This company will provide such facilities.
I think this company is to be commended on its leadership and private initiative in providing a need in our private enterprise, permitting our companies to sell their goods abroad without waiting upon government action in this connection. The interested parties are banding together to fulfil this great need in our export trade.

maintopic: EXPORT FINANCE CORPORATION OF CANADA LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the bill before the house this afternoon marks a very significant development in Canada's trading relationships with the rest of the world. As I listened to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir) who sponsored the bill, outlining the discussion that took place in the other place it seemed remarkable to me that we have been so long delayed in having private participation in this important activity. During recent years the whole trading position of Canada with respect to the rest of the world has changed dramatically, and there has been a golden opportunity for private initiative and enterprise to take a constructive role. Yet it has remained until this occasion for the first halting steps to take place in this worthwhile field of endeavour.
During the past decade or so the government of Canada has taken on many activities to facilitate Canada's trading position with respect to the rest of the world, but there has been a vacuum in this area. It seems to me this is going to be merely the beginning of a further step forward in Canada's trading position.
As a western member I am especially interested in this development, of course, because many of the economic problems that are ours on the prairies can only be resolved as we move as a nation, as a government and as private citizens, to develop and expand our trading activities in other parts of the world.
We in the west have surplus agricultural products to contend with from time to time. Of course, this applies to other agricultural areas in Canada. It seems to me, that the activities of this new Export Finance Corporation can be very usefully directed toward helping in a small way to correct the economic imbalance of the prairies.
As I understand the remarks of the hon. member who sponsors this bill, it relates itself to agricultural products as well as to manufactured articles and industrial articles generally. It also seems to me that this is about the best kind of credit for export and import purposes that could be

made available. We have in Canada as a crown activity the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. I presume that any loans taken up by both exporters and importers under the operations of this company will be insurable by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. This suggests that there is absolutely no risk involved at all for those who want the facilities of this corporation. When that fact is generally known I am sure it will be a further incentive to those who wish to make use of the financial operations of the corporation.
I notice that in the reference to the interest rates the observation is made that these will be flexible; that there is no fixed interest charge for the operations of loans under this corporation. I would only suggest, that I trust the interest rates will be reasonable and in line with prevailing rates. It seems to me that any financial activity is discouraged or encouraged largely by the interest rates established. In view of the flexibility that is available to those who will be carrying on the operations of this corporation I would presume that they will take an entirely reasonable approach. I hope, too, that the inauguration of this company will be just the beginning of similar activities along these lines.
If Canada is to correct the imbalance of her trading relations that have developed in a move toward the position of a world trader, it is going to require all the ingenuity and all the energy of private citizens everywhere, as well as the operations already supported by the government of Canada.
Again, I would say that as a member from western Canada it would seem to me that this is a large contribution to make in encouraging our agricultural industry, in assisting toward diversification and thus resolving one of our basic problems, and also -and perhaps this is even more important because it is a new aspect of industrial activity on the prairies-encouraging the growing activities of our manufacturing industries in the west by providing further outlets for their products in the foreign markets of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join other hon. members in congratulating the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir). I was particularly interested in his statement concerning one of the witnesses who appeared before the investigating committee of the other place, a highly trained and qualified engineer who said that the advertising of Canadian engineering skill abroad had opened up tremendous export
Export Finance Corporation opportunities to Canadian manufacturing concerns but unfortunately because of the credit restrictions which are naturally imposed by Canadian banking firms the manufacturers have been unable to take advantage of these opportunities in foreign countries. The establishment of such a company is provided for by the bill, a company which will advance to manufacturing concerns possibly very large amounts of money, will give the Canadian people a greater degree of employment than they have had in the past. A lot of these projects referred to by the hon. member involve large orders for machinery and equipment and naturally under present regulations the manufacturer cannot afford to extend long term credit to the country ordering the goods.
Under the bill the Export Finance Corporation of Canada will be permitted to advance to manufacturers the capital expenditures required. Testimony was given by the same person before the committee of the other place that in the past two years somewhere between $6 million and $28 million in orders for heavy equipment had been lost to Canadian industry simply because we had no such credit corporation.
In	France and Germany bankers,
machinery suppliers, general contractors and engineering firms have pooled their resources to establish a revolving fund and in this way have overcome the problem. In his evidence this man stated that they had investigated an order for machinery in Brazil, machinery which could have been made in Canada involving approximately $12 million. That is a tremendous amount of money for a single order. He also stated that he had discovered that there was strong good will toward Canada and Canadians especially in the so-called underdeveloped nations. He also went on to refer to a tremendous order in Chile involving some $17 million which could have been manufactured in Canada but because of the lack of credit facilities to the companies concerned was lost. There was a recent engineering project in Mexico City and the authorities there were quite willing to place the order with Canadian manufacturers even at a higher figure than would have been the case elsewhere but although approximately $15 million was involved the order was lost by Canadian manufacturers and employees.
The capitalization is only $50 million and I feel sure that within the next two years we will find that with respect to heavy industry alone this sum will be oversubscribed. I admit, as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) says, that perhaps the company is not running too much of a risk

Private Bills-Divorce
because of our Export Credits Insurance Act. However, any venture involving such large sums carries with it a certain amount of risk and I am not prepared to quarrel with this company at all with respect to any reasonable sum which they will charge for the use of the money, nor am I prepared to quarrel with the government's present policy with regard to the Export Credits Insurance Act.
We must remember that immediately south of us in the United States there is a government agency which looks after most large orders involving the export of machinery. I refer to the United States export-import bank. From what I have read in the newspapers I understand that in the past some difficulties have been encountered by business in floating loans through the Canadian government agency. However, with this private corporation in operation there will at least be no political implications whatsoever.
I would expect that with this corporation in operation there would be more processing of our raw materials before export. I certainly agree wholeheartedly with the sponsor of the bill that this is an excellent move and that it would be a good thing for the house to pass the bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. S-17, to incorporate Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited, involves such an important principle and is of such purport that it should have been introduced as a government measure for the establishment of a crown corporation or agency. However, in view of the fact that the government has given no indication of any such intention and has nothing in mind as far as we know that would cover the provisions of this bill and in view of the fact that there is a need for such an operation, let me say as clearly as I can, since everybody seems to support the bill and nobody objects to it, let us put it to a vote.

Mr. Speaker, this group of bills we are considering today brings us a little over the halfway mark in the amount of work in this particular field that will confront the House of Commons this session. There are a few points with which I should like to deal this afternoon in moving the second reading of these bills, points which are directly related to individual cases that are to be found amongst the group we are considering.
Since the house earlier today heard hymns of praise from various members in favour of the women's institutes, I should like to refer to something absolutely new that has crept into the divorce practice in the province which sends its cases to us. For the first time, so far as I am aware, we have had the appearance of lady detectives before a parliamentary committee. These charming creatures ordinarily operate in civil life, in one instance as a saleslady and in the other instance as a photographer. They have chosen to supplement their income by doing a bit of investigating. They appeared, for those members who are curious, in those cases presented in the 180th report of the committee of the other place which deals with these cases.
It might be refreshing, Mr. Speaker, to put into the record some brief extracts from the testimony of these ladies.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Has the hon. member got photographs of the ladies that he would like to put in Hansard.'!

No, but I daresay they would be very photogenic. It is difficult, under the circumstances, to read the testimony of one of these private eyes because she uses such phrases as, "I says", and other mutilations of the English language which seem to suggest a greater familiarity with the work of Mickey Spillane than with the ordinary rules of grammar.
However, I did not intend to comment on that, but rather to answer the point I am sure most of the members of the house will be asking and that is, how did these ladies turn out as witnesses? It must be said for them that they brought their cases to a very successful conclusion. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that there are certain rules of law which
Private Bills-Divorce
frown on hearsay evidence and which, in short, tend to keep witnesses right to the point of the case. I must say that the ladies did manage to put a great deal of hearsay evidence on the record before the committee of the other place. I can only presume that the gentlemen who heard the evidence were extraordinarily gallant that day and gave a certain leeway to these lady detectives.
For example, I might say that the elder of the lady detectives was waiting outside an apartment where the rendezvous was taking place between the respondent and the co-respondent. This is the evidence she gave to the Senate committee, and I cite this as an example of the kind of hearsay evidence that crept into the record:
Around 6, not more alter 6, I saw that man coming around the street and he came through the building and he went to his apartment, same apartment; and we sat down and wait; it was a warm, warm day in August. I said, "Well, we can have lunch; they will have their supper, I suppose;"-
That is quite irrelevant, but the senators allowed it to go on the record. Then, they had a cup of tea and came back a few minutes afterwards. By this time it was 7.30 and the ladies waited around till 10 or 11 at night. Then, they marched in upon their quarry at 11.30. Then, continuing to quote from the testimony of the elder of the two detectives, I read:
-I said to my witness, "It is O.K.; it is late enough"; because it is a big apartment, ol course, and I knew before that.
They went in, and carried out this investigation very well. Indeed, they acted just like men detectives. Once the door was opened, one of them stuck her foot in it so it could not be closed, and they both marched in. The younger lady detective got a little bit excited and did not make all the notes she should have made as to what was observed. While both of them were lady detectives, they did not seem to be agreed as to the nightdress that was worn by the co-respondent. One said she had a nightgown or the top part of pyjamas, but the other one was not sure.
This case is one of several in which certain people connected therewith have taken up detective occupations at night, forsaking such ordinary occupations as lingerie salesman, insurance adjuster and other jobs. There have been any number who have appeared before parliament to give evidence in cases, including several in the group of cases we are considering now. Quite a number of these amateur detectives do not have licences issued by either the provincial or municipal authorities in Quebec. This, to me, seems to be a growing practice. Anybody in Montreal can try his hand at playing detective, without going

Private Bills-Divorce
through the legal formalities of being licensed to do so. I merely draw this to the attention of the people in Quebec because they may wish to consider this problem.
Also included in the cases before us this afternoon are several which indicate that there may be a new pattern developing in the city of Montreal, a sort of new switch on the motel and hotel type of case that has bothered parliament for some years. In making a check of these cases to try to analyse the pattern developing I found the same lawyers, the same firm of detectives and sometimes the same hotels or motels were involved. However, I came upon a curious set of cases in this particular batch in which the same lawyer, the same detectives were always involved; the evidence was very much the same, but in each case the rendezvous had occurred in some young lady's apartment. It was not the same young lady in each case, but it was an apartment. It seems to me that the people down there who connive and contrive at these particular cases have hit upon this as a new modus operandi to try to pull the wool over the eyes of the members in the other place and the members in this House of Commons. It would seem they make arrangements with the young women so that the husband goes to an apartment instead of a hotel or a motel. This will be an extraordinarily difficult thing to check, but nonetheless it seems to have developed into a set pattern. There may be attempts to impose on parliament-
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit another question? Can the hon. gentleman tell us whether he is moving the adoption of these bills or speaking against them?

The answer to this question could lead me into a very philosophic discussion about the role of the chairman of the miscellaneous private bills committee.
The practice was developed years ago of having the chairman on the committee act as sponsor for all these bills. It made things somewhat easier than would be the case with lawyers or petitioners running around badgering members of parliament to sponsor particular bills before parliament. I am in a curious position. My name is down as sponsor for each one of these divorce bills. Three hundred or so of these bills were dealt with last year and I suspect that 400 will be dealt with this year. I conscientiously go through them so that if other members should raise questions about them I will be able to give some assistance to the house or to the committee if we are in committee on them.
Does not the sponsor have to stand behind every fact of the bill that he introduces?
I hope not.
It would be most interesting if the hon. member could do that.

If that is my position as sponsor, I would have no recourse than to walk out of the House of Commons. I could not in conscience say that it was my duty to stand behind every statement of fact or every statement of a witness before the committee of the other place nor do I conceive that to be my duty either.
You could not do it anyway.

As I see it, the position of myself, both as sponsor and as chairman of the committee which has to deal with these cases, is that when I speak to the house I must speak more in the role of chairman than as sponsor. Perhaps I am wrong, but that is the way I see it.
There is a case here, namely Bill SD-178, in which the co-respondent and the respondent went to a motel on what one detective described as an extremely snowy night. I think that case will deserve particular consideration in committee. It seems to have a rather unpleasant odour about it. But in accordance with the practice of the house, which is on second reading to treat more with the principle than with the particulars of the individual bill, I am asking that these bills be given second reading. We shall have an opportunity to consider the more difficult cases in our committee where, I might say, we are already holding up the eleven bills for special consideration.
